blood.glucose_mg_per_dL.note: Basal glucose Gb in the minimal model.

cardio.heartRateIntrinsic_bpm.note: Denervated SA node rate; both reflex limbs act on this.

cardio.lv.Emax_mmHg_per_mL.note: Human LV end-systolic elastance, normal range 2-3.

cardio.lv.Emin_mmHg_per_mL.note: Diastolic (passive) elastance. 0.075 puts end-diastolic pressure at about 8 mmHg when end-diastolic volume is 120 mL, which is the normal filling pressure.

cardio.lv.V0_mL.note: Unstressed LV volume, the ESPVR volume-axis intercept.

cardio.activation.systolicFraction.note: Systolic duration ~ 0.3 x RR at 72 bpm; shortens with rate via the Bazett-like scaling below.

cardio.activation.hill1_exponent.note: Rising-limb exponent of the double-Hill activation e(t). Mynard reports the activation shape rather than this coefficient directly; the value is the one that reproduces his published curve.

cardio.activation.hill2_exponent.note: Falling-limb exponent. Much larger than the rising one, which is what makes systolic contraction fast and diastolic relaxation slow — a symmetric activation reads as fake immediately.

cardio.activation.tau1_fraction.note: Rising-limb time constant as a fraction of the reference R-R interval, from the same published activation curve.

cardio.activation.tau2_fraction.note: Falling-limb time constant as a fraction of the reference R-R interval.

cardio.wk.C_mL_per_mmHg.note: Total arterial compliance. Stergiopulos reports 1.0-2.0 mL/mmHg for adults; 1.30 is the value inside that range at which the model reproduces a 48 mmHg pulse pressure at a 78 mL stroke volume.

cardio.wk.R_mmHg_s_per_mL.note: Peripheral resistance from MAP 92, RAP 4, CO 5 L/min: (92-4)/83.3 mL/s.

cardio.venous.unstressedVolume_mL.note: Venous reservoir that carries no pressure; sympathetic tone recruits it. Calibrated within the published 60-75% of total blood volume so that the closed loop settles at a textbook resting point: BP 120/72, CO 5.4 L/min, EDV 120 mL, CVP 5 mmHg.

cardio.venous.R_mmHg_s_per_mL.note: Resistance to venous return. Together with the unstressed volume above it sets where the venous-return and cardiac-output curves intersect, which is what fixes resting cardiac output.

cardio.aorta.unstressedVolume_mL.note: Arterial tree holds about 900 mL at a mean pressure of 92 mmHg with a compliance of 1.6 mL/mmHg, so 750 mL of it carries no pressure.

cardio.pulmArt.unstressedVolume_mL.note: Pulmonary artery holds about 130 mL at a mean pressure of 15 mmHg with a compliance of 4.3 mL/mmHg, so half of it carries no pressure.

cardio.pulmVein.unstressedVolume_mL.note: Total pulmonary blood volume is about 450 mL; this is the share of the venous half that carries no pressure.

cardio.pulmVein.R_mmHg_s_per_mL.note: Pulmonary vein to left atrium. Small, because the gradient from wedge pressure to left atrial pressure is only a millimetre or two of mercury at rest.

cardio.valve.R_mmHg_s_per_mL.note: Forward resistance of a competent valve.

cardio.valve.regurgitantR_mmHg_s_per_mL.note: Closed valve modelled as a very large but finite resistance to keep the ODE non-stiff.

baroreflex.setpoint_mmHg.note: Carotid sinus pressure at the sigmoid midpoint.

baroreflex.sympDelay_s.note: Pure transport delay on the sympathetic limb.

baroreflex.vagalTau_s.note: Vagal limb is fast: this is why HR responds within one or two beats.

baroreflex.gainHR_sym_bpm.note: Calibrated in the closed loop so resting HR is 72 at balanced tone and class-III haemorrhage drives it to ~140, the textbook response. Ursino supplies the reflex structure; this gain is our fit to it.

baroreflex.gainHR_vagal_bpm.note: Calibrated so full vagal tone produces the ~30 bpm bradycardia seen with carotid sinus massage.

baroreflex.gainContractility.note: Full sympathetic drive raises Emax about 60%.

baroreflex.gainResistance.note: Full sympathetic drive raises SVR about 70%.

baroreflex.gainVenousTone_mL.note: Unstressed venous volume recruited at full sympathetic drive.

ecg.baselineWander_mV.note: z0 amplitude; carries respiratory sinus arrhythmia.

ecg.amplitudeGain.note: The McSharry z variable is dimensionless; the paper scales its output to a physiological range rather than producing millivolts directly. The excursion produced by one Gaussian event is a*b^2/omega, so with the published a=30 and b=0.1 the raw R wave is about 0.048 units. This gain puts it at 1.2 mV, which is a normal lead-II R wave.

ecg.referenceRate_bpm.note: The raw model's amplitude scales as 1/omega, so an untreated trace would halve its R wave when the heart rate doubled. Real R-wave amplitude does not depend on rate. The event sum is therefore scaled by omega/omega_ref, which cancels the dependence and leaves the published parameters meaning what they mean at 60 bpm.

ecg.rsaFraction.note: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia: RR modulation amplitude at the respiratory rate.

resp.pio2_mmHg.note: (760 - 47) x 0.2095 at sea level, body temperature, saturated.

resp.pao2_mmHg.note: Arterial; alveolar is ~104, the difference is the A-a gradient.

resp.centralChemoGain_L_per_min_per_mmHg.note: Ventilatory response slope to CO2, awake adult.

resp.centralChemoThreshold_mmHg.note: Apnoeic threshold; below this, CO2 drive is zero.

resp.peripheralChemoThreshold_mmHg.note: Hypoxic drive only becomes significant below this.

resp.peripheralChemoGain_L_per_min.note: Ventilation at full hypoxic drive. The carotid body response is steeply non-linear below 60 mmHg; this is the asymptote it approaches, and the square law in systems/respiratory.ts is the approach to it.

immune.cd4Baseline_per_uL.note: Normal adult CD4+ T lymphocyte count. The reference the HIV model falls from; below 200 defines AIDS.

resp.chemoVentilationCeiling_L_per_min.note: The ventilatory response to CO2 is linear over the physiological range and then FLATTENS; it does not rise without limit. This is the plateau the combined chemoreflex approaches, applied as a saturating hyperbola in systems/respiratory.ts. Documented as derived for the same reason as the peripheral gain: the textbook curve is read as an asymptote rather than published as one number. Without a ceiling the reflex could manufacture 50 L/min of drive from a PaCO2 of 52, which is what let a body in cardiac arrest go on breathing.

resp.co2NarcosisThreshold_mmHg.note: Above roughly this tension carbon dioxide begins to DEPRESS the respiratory centre rather than stimulate it. The stimulant limb and the narcotic limb are the same molecule at different concentrations.

resp.co2NarcosisAbolished_mmHg.note: Tension at which central depression is complete and CO2 drive is abolished. Read off the narcosis/coma range rather than published as a single figure; the ramp between this and the threshold is linear.

resp.co2SolubilityFactor.note: CO2 solubility in plasma at 37 C.

fluid.interstitialVolume_mL.note: Extracellular fluid is about 14 L in a 70 kg adult: roughly 3 L of plasma and the rest interstitial. This compartment is what defends plasma volume.

fluid.insensibleLoss_mL_per_min.note: About 1 L/day from skin and the respiratory tract. Not urine, and not regulated.

fluid.obligateIntake_mL_per_min.note: About 2.4 L/day from drink, food water and metabolic water. At baseline this exactly balances urine plus insensible loss, which is what makes a resting body weight-stable. See docs/MODEL_LIMITATIONS.md: the body is modelled as drinking to thirst, not on a schedule.

fluid.transcapillaryRefillTau_min.note: Time constant of plasma volume restitution from the interstitium after a volume loss. This is why a bled subject partly recovers their blood pressure over the following half hour without any fluid being given.

renal.autoregLow_mmHg.note: Lower limit of myogenic + tubuloglomerular autoregulation.

renal.autoregSharpness.note: Logistic steepness of the fall-off outside the plateau.

gi.gastricEmptyingHalfTime_min.note: t-half for a standard liquid/semisolid meal.

gi.gastricEmptyingBeta.note: Power-exponential shape parameter; >1 produces the observed initial lag.

gi.fatEmptyingDelayFactor_per_gram.unit: fraction increase in t-half per g fat
gi.fatEmptyingDelayFactor_per_gram.note: Fat is the strongest inhibitor of gastric emptying.

gi.gastricAcidSecretion_mEq_per_h.note: Basal acid output; peaks around 20 mEq/h stimulated.

gi.mealBufferCapacity_mEq_per_g_protein.note: Protein is the dominant dietary buffer.

gi.transitTime_min.note: Stomach is null because its residence time is computed by the Elashoff model, not fixed.

gi.glucoseAbsorption_mg_per_min_max.note: SGLT1-limited; ~ 120 g/h upper bound in the proximal small bowel.

gi.segmentLength_m.note: Sums to about 8.4 m of tract; the popular '30 feet' figure is post-mortem, unconstrained by muscle tone.

metabolic.insulinSecretionGain.note: Replaces the minimal model's gamma*(G-h)*t secretion term, which is only defined for a single IVGTT. Calibrated so a post-prandial glucose of 140 mg/dL yields a steady-state insulin of about 60 uU/mL against the model's own clearance n.

thermal.regulatoryGain_per_C.note: Proportional thermoregulation: heat loss rises above the set point through sweating and skin vasodilation, and falls below it through vasoconstriction. Without this the model has no defended temperature at all, only an equilibrium.

thermal.ambientTemp_C.note: Room temperature for the scenario; not a measured physiological value.

thermal.heatLossCoefficient_W_per_C.note: Combined convective, radiative and evaporative loss at neutral skin blood flow. Solved so that 84 W of basal heat production is exactly balanced at 37.0 C against a 22 C ambient: any other value makes core temperature drift all day, which the 24-hour homeostasis test catches.

neuro.consciousnessLossCBF_fraction.note: Syncope threshold; below this, level of consciousness falls.

arrest.cprStrokeVolumeFraction.note: Optimal manual compressions generate roughly a quarter to a third of normal cardiac OUTPUT. Note the unit: at 110 compressions per minute against a resting rate of 66, 27% of normal output is only about 13 mL per compression, which is 17% of a normal 78 mL stroke volume. Reading the figure as 27% of stroke VOLUME doubles the delivered flow and produces coronary pressures no manual CPR achieves.

arrest.cprPressureAmplitude_mmHg.note: Peak intrathoracic pressure from a 5-6 cm compression. Calibrated in tests/sim/arrest.test.ts so the thoracic pump delivers a cardiac output of 25-30% of normal at 110 compressions per minute.

arrest.cprArterialTransmission.note: Fraction of the compression pressure transmitted to the arterial side. The thoracic aorta is inside the chest and is squeezed too, so only part of the compression appears as a driving gradient. Omitting it entirely made CPR an implausibly efficient pump.

arrest.cprVenousTransmission.note: The great veins are intrathoracic as well. Valves at the thoracic inlet stop the pressure being transmitted onward to the neck, which is what rectifies the thoracic pump into forward flow.

arrest.cprDownstrokeDuration_s.note: A 50% duty cycle at 110 compressions per minute.

arrest.cprCompressionDecay_s.note: Coronary perfusion decays this fast when compressions pause.

arrest.cppRosc_mmHg.note: Coronary perfusion pressure below which defibrillation rarely succeeds.

arrest.defibBaseSuccess_vfib.note: First-shock termination of VF with a biphasic device, short downtime.

arrest.defibDowntimeHalfLife_s.note: Shockability decays with untreated downtime; 7-10% per minute survival decrement.

sim.ecgSubsteps.note: The McSharry ODEs are stiffer than the rest; sub-step at dt/4 (spec 4.1).

sim.snapshotRate_Hz.note: Object snapshots to the renderer and the interface. Fast enough that interpolation between two of them is invisible, slow enough that structured cloning does not dominate the worker.

sim.conditionHysteresis.note: +/-3% dead band so condition tags do not flicker (spec 4.8).

sim.maxTimeScale.note: Fastest offered time scale. 300x turns a four-hour oral distribution curve into forty-eight seconds, which is what makes a pharmacokinetic tail something a user will actually watch.

resp.fio2RoomAir.note: Oxygen fraction of dry atmospheric air.

resp.waterVapour_mmHg.note: Saturated water vapour pressure at 37 C. Inspired gas is humidified before it reaches the alveoli, so this is subtracted from barometric pressure before the oxygen fraction is applied.

env.lapseCoefficient_per_m.note: Coefficient of the tropospheric barometric formula P = P0 (1 - k h)^n. Real pressure at a given altitude varies with latitude and season: West measured 253 mmHg on the summit of Everest where this formula gives about 236.

env.pressureExponent.note: Exponent of the tropospheric barometric formula.

blood.ketones_mmol_per_L.note: Fed-state total ketone bodies are around 0.1 mmol/L; values above 0.5 indicate ketosis and above 3 are diagnostic of ketoacidosis.

blood.platelets_10e9_per_L.note: Midpoint of the normal platelet count range (150-400 x10^9/L).

blood.apttNormal_s.note: Midpoint of the usual reference interval for the activated partial thromboplastin time (about 25-35 s); laboratories set their own.

immune.wbcBaseline_10e9_per_L.note: Normal adult white cell count, about 7000 per microlitre.

immune.crpBaseline_mg_per_L.note: Median C-reactive protein in healthy young adults. Rises within 6 h of an inflammatory stimulus and peaks at about 48 h; plasma half-life about 19 h.

immune.crpHalfLife_h.note: Plasma half-life of CRP, constant in health and disease, so the level is set entirely by synthesis rate.

immune.crpMax_mg_per_L.note: Upper end of the CRP levels seen in severe bacterial infection (Pepys reports increases of up to 10,000-fold from the median); used as the ceiling the acute-phase response saturates toward.

immune.wbcMax_10e9_per_L.note: A marked neutrophil leucocytosis in severe bacterial infection; the ceiling the count saturates toward at full immune activation.

neuro.pupilBaseline_mm.note: Resting pupil diameter in ordinary room light, within the 1.5-8 mm physiological range the iris can span.

neuro.pupilMin_mm.note: Smallest pupil the sphincter pupillae produces (pinpoint).

neuro.pupilMax_mm.note: Largest pupil the dilator pupillae produces.

acidbase.pK.note: Apparent pK of the carbonic acid/bicarbonate system in plasma, for the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation.

acidbase.acuteHco3PerPaco2.note: Acute respiratory acidosis: bicarbonate rises about 1 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2, from non-bicarbonate (mostly haemoglobin) buffering. Adrogue and Madias give 0.2 per mmHg for acute respiratory ALKALOSIS; the single slope is kept and the asymmetry noted.

acidbase.chronicHco3PerPaco2.note: Chronic respiratory acidosis: after renal adaptation bicarbonate rises about 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg PaCO2.

acidbase.renalCompensationTau_h.note: Renal adaptation to a sustained PaCO2 change is complete in 3-5 days; a first-order lag with a one-day time constant is 95 % complete by day three.

acidbase.ventilatoryCompensationAcidosis.note: Metabolic acidosis: PaCO2 falls about 1.2 mmHg for every 1 mEq/L fall in bicarbonate (equivalently Winters' formula, Albert 1967). The chemoreflex term that produces this is calibrated to this slope, not tuned to a trace.

acidbase.ventilatoryCompensationAlkalosi.note: Metabolic alkalosis: PaCO2 rises about 0.7 mmHg per 1 mEq/L rise in bicarbonate.

acidbase.metabolicRecoveryTau_h.note: Renal regeneration or excretion of bicarbonate after a fixed acid or alkali load is removed takes days; same one-day first-order lag as the respiratory compensation, because it is the same organ doing the same job.

myocardium.coronaryFlowReserve.note: Coronary blood flow can rise three- to four-fold above resting in strenuous exercise; midpoint taken. This is the headroom the heart has to answer hypoxaemia by vasodilating before it runs short of oxygen.

myocardium.restingO2Extraction.note: The resting heart already removes about 70 % of the oxygen in coronary arterial blood, far more than any other organ, which is why it can answer a fall in oxygen content only with more flow, not more extraction.

myocardium.maxO2Extraction.note: Ceiling on myocardial oxygen extraction. Extraction cannot reach 100 % because oxygen only diffuses out of the capillary down a pressure gradient; 90 % leaves coronary venous PO2 near the floor at which diffusion still supplies the myocyte. Not a measured figure.

myocardium.referenceCpp_mmHg.note: Normal coronary perfusion pressure: aortic diastolic pressure (about 80 mmHg) less right atrial pressure (0-10 mmHg). The flow the reserve multiplies is taken as proportional to perfusion pressure relative to this.

myocardium.arrestedDemandFraction.note: Oxygen consumption of a non-beating myocardium as a fraction of a working one. The basal, non-contractile metabolism of heart muscle is a small fraction of total consumption; one fifth is an order-of-magnitude choice, stated as such.

myocardium.hypoxiaTau_s.note: Time constant with which myocardial oxygenation follows supply. Myoglobin and dissolved oxygen in the myocardium sustain aerobic work for only seconds, so the lag is short; the exact figure is a modelling choice.

myocardium.peaAfterProfoundHypoxia_s.note: Seconds of near-total myocardial hypoxia (supply below a tenth of demand) before an organised rhythm stops producing a pulse. Hypoxic arrests present as bradycardia degenerating to PEA rather than VF; the timing is a modelling choice.

myocardium.asystoleAfterPea_s.note: Further seconds of profound hypoxia in PEA before electrical activity fails too. Untreated PEA degrades to asystole over minutes; the figure is a modelling choice.

myocardium.roscAfterReoxygenation_s.note: Seconds of restored myocardial oxygenation (supply at least matching demand) needed before a PEA heart resumes effective contraction. Treating the cause is what restores a pulse in PEA; the dwell stops a single good compression from counting as ROSC.

posture.standingPooling_mL.note: On standing, gravity displaces about 500-1000 mL of blood into the veins of the legs and splanchnic bed; the lower bound is used for a healthy, well-toned subject.

posture.sittingPoolingFraction.note: Sitting puts roughly half the vertical column below the heart that standing does; half the standing volume is an estimate on that geometry, not a measurement.

posture.poolingTau_s.note: Most gravitational pooling happens within the first 10-30 s of standing, which is why initial orthostatic hypotension appears in that window.

thermal.shiveringMaxRise.note: Maximal shivering raises heat production to four to five times basal; +3 (four times basal) is used.

thermal.shiveringSpan_C.note: Core-temperature fall below the set point at which shivering is maximal. Shivering rises proportionally below the set point; the span over which it saturates is a modelling choice.

thermal.latentHeat_kJ_per_g.note: Heat lost per gram of sweat evaporated: 0.58 kcal/g.

thermal.maxSweatRate_mL_per_h.note: Sweat rates in exercising and heat-exposed adults range from about 0.5 to 2 L/h; 1 L/h is used as the sustainable maximum for an unacclimatised adult. Evaporative heat loss at this rate is about 675 W.

thermal.sweatSpan_C.note: Core-temperature rise above the set point at which sweating reaches its maximum. Sweating rises steeply with core temperature; the one-degree span is a modelling choice.

neuro.seizureDuration_s.note: Median duration of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure recorded in an epilepsy monitoring unit is about one minute; seizures beyond five minutes are unlikely to stop on their own.

neuro.postictalRefractory_s.note: Refractory period after a seizure before the model will let another begin from the same provocation. A modelling choice that stops a borderline threshold producing a seizure every tick.

neuro.seizureGlucose_mg_per_dL.note: Neuroglycopenic seizures become likely as glucose falls toward 40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L).

neuro.seizureSodium_mEq_per_L.note: Seizures are a feature of acute hyponatraemia below about 120 mEq/L.

neuro.seizureTemperature_C.note: Core temperature at which hyperthermic seizures become likely.

gi.vomitThreshold.note: Nausea index (0..1 on the effect bus) above which emesis occurs. The bus carries nausea as a dimensionless drive; the threshold is a modelling choice.

gi.vomitEpisode_s.note: Duration of one bout of vomiting.

gi.vomitInterval_s.note: Minimum interval between vomiting bouts while nausea persists.

coag.bleedingTime_min.note: Normal bleeding time is 1-6 minutes; the midpoint sets how fast haemostasis builds on a bleed.

coag.largeBleedRate_mL_per_min.note: Bleed rate at which clot holds only half of it even with normal clotting. Haemostasis stops capillary and small-vessel bleeding and fails against arterial bleeding; the crossover is a modelling choice.

coag.inrExponent.note: INR is modelled as 1 / (clotting-factor activity) ^ n. With n = 1 a factor activity of 40 % gives an INR of 2.5, inside the therapeutic 2-3 band in which vitamin K-dependent factor activity is in the region of 30-40 %; a modelling choice anchored to that correspondence.

airway.histamineHalfLife_s.note: Plasma histamine is cleared within minutes; a two-minute half-life for circulating mast-cell mediator activity is a modelling choice. Release continues from degranulating mast cells for longer, carried separately.

airway.mastCellReleaseTau_s.note: Time constant over which a sensitised mast-cell population discharges after an exposure. Anaphylaxis evolves over minutes to tens of minutes; a modelling choice.

airway.histamineSystemicResistanceFall.note: Fall in systemic resistance at full mast-cell mediator activity, from histamine, leukotrienes and platelet-activating factor together; distributive shock. H1 blockade removes only the histamine share, which is why antihistamines do not treat anaphylactic shock.

airway.histamineBronchoconstriction.note: Airway narrowing at full mast-cell mediator activity.

airway.histaminePermeabilityRise.note: Rise in capillary permeability at full mediator activity: the plasma leak of anaphylaxis, sized to match the inflammatory leak in pathology.json.

resp.physiologicalShunt.note: Normal venous admixture: bronchial and Thebesian venous drainage plus the ventilation-perfusion scatter of a healthy lung, lumped as a true shunt. About 2-3 % reproduces the normal alveolar-arterial PO2 difference of 5-10 mmHg through the shunt equation.

resp.apnoeaPaco2Rise_mmHg_per_min.note: Steady rate of rise of PaCO2 during complete airway obstruction after the first minute (the first minute adds about 12 mmHg as lung and blood equilibrate with mixed venous blood).

resp.co2Capacitance_mmHg_per_L.unit: mmHg per L of CO2 retained
resp.co2Capacitance_mmHg_per_L.note: Apnoeic rise rate divided by resting CO2 production (3.4 mmHg/min / 0.2 L/min). This is the whole-body CO2 store that limits how fast PaCO2 can climb when ventilation falls short of production; the fast lag toward the ventilation-equation target still governs any FALL, which is limited only by lung washout.

resp.alveolarGasVolume_mL.note: Gas volume the alveolar oxygen balance is taken over: functional residual capacity. The oxygen in it is the store that lets a breath-hold last a minute on air and eight after breathing pure oxygen.

acidbase.chemoStimulusAcidosis_mmHg_per_.unit: mmHg PaCO2-equivalent per mEq/L HCO3 deficit
acidbase.chemoStimulusAcidosis_mmHg_per_.note: Metabolic acidosis adds this to the CO2 stimulus per mEq/L bicarbonate deficit, driving compensatory hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing). Calibrated against Winters formula: at HCO3 12 the model settles at PaCO2 26 (Winters 26 +/- 2), at HCO3 16 at PaCO2 30 (Winters 32). tests/sim/acidbase.test.ts asserts it.

acidbase.chemoStimulusAlkalosis_mmHg_per.unit: mmHg PaCO2-equivalent per mEq/L HCO3 excess
acidbase.chemoStimulusAlkalosis_mmHg_per.note: Metabolic alkalosis subtracts from the CO2 stimulus per mEq/L bicarbonate excess. Weaker than the acidosis limb here and clinically, because hypoventilation costs oxygenation, so respiratory compensation for a metabolic alkalosis is the least reliable of the four disorders.

blood.plateletLifespan_days.note: Circulating platelet lifespan, 8-10 days; sets how slowly the count answers a change in production or destruction.

neuro.seizureLactateRise_mmol_per_L_per_.note: Rate of lactate accumulation during the tonic-clonic phase of a generalised seizure, from the near-total anaerobic metabolism of maximally contracting muscle; a post-ictal lactate above 5 mmol/L that clears within an hour is characteristic.

acidbase.myocardialDepressionOnset_pH.note: pH below which myocardial contractility begins to fall measurably; severe acidaemia (pH < 7.1-7.2) depresses cardiac contractility and blunts the response to catecholamines.

acidbase.contractilityLossPerPh.note: Slope of contractility loss below the onset pH: at pH 7.0 (0.2 below onset) contractility is reduced about 30 %. An order-of-magnitude choice consistent with the experimental depression of cardiac function in acidaemia, stated as such.

fluid.stoolNa_mEq_per_L.note: Sodium concentration of cholera stool in adults; the losses are nearly isotonic, which is why saline-based rehydration works.

fluid.stoolK_mEq_per_L.note: Potassium concentration of cholera stool; the potassium loss is proportionally greater than plasma, which is why cholera causes hypokalaemia.

fluid.stoolHco3_mEq_per_L.note: Bicarbonate concentration of cholera stool; losing it is the metabolic acidosis of severe cholera.

fluid.sweatNa_mEq_per_L.note: Sodium concentration of sweat in an unacclimatised adult (range 20-80 mEq/L); hypotonic, so heavy sweating without salt causes hypernatraemia.

resp.restingPaco2_mmHg.note: The PaCO2 this model's chemoreflex loop settles at when awake and at rest: the sourced central-chemoreceptor threshold (37) plus the baseline drive together hold the operating point just below the textbook 40. Used as the reference for cerebral CO2 reactivity so a resting body reads as fully alert. The offset from 40 is a property of the loop, recorded here rather than hidden.

resp.stagnantArterialTau_min.note: Time constant over which arterial blood equilibrates toward venous oxygen content when the circulation has stopped. Desaturation after a cardiac arrest is observed over one to two minutes; the exact constant is a modelling choice, chosen so an unperfused body desaturates over that window rather than holding its last saturation indefinitely.

metabolic.maxInsulinGlucoseDisposal_mg_p.note: Maximal insulin-stimulated whole-body glucose disposal in healthy adults under the euglycaemic clamp, reached at plasma insulin in the hundreds of uU/mL; the upper end of the reported 10-15 mg/kg/min range is used so that ordinary meal insulin stays below the ceiling and only a supraphysiological dose meets it.
